Control your phone with the hand you already know.

Tactiq is a smart ring that gives blind and low-vision people a quiet, one-handed way to control their phone. Tap a point on your fingers, and VoiceOver or TalkBack carries out the command.

Where it fits in a day

Not a new way to live — a quieter way to do the small things a phone already does.

One hand is already busy

A cane or a guide-dog harness occupies one hand outdoors. Tactiq puts every command on the free hand, so nothing has to be put down.

A call in a loud place

On a train platform, voice control fails and a touchscreen demands attention. A tap on the index finger answers the call; a tap below it declines.

Moving through a screen reader, silently

Next, previous, read again, confirm — the four moves screen-reader users repeat hundreds of times a day, without speaking aloud or finding a spot on glass.

How it works

One continuous movement of the hand, from intention to confirmation. The design target is at most one false activation per hour — the squeeze is what stops taps from firing accidentally.

  1. 1

    Squeeze

    A deliberate squeeze of the ring body wakes it and opens a short command window.

  2. 2

    Tap

    Your thumb taps one of eight contact points on the tips and bases of your fingers.

  3. 3

    Detect

    The ring senses which point was touched, on-device — no camera, no microphone.

  4. 4

    Act

    Your phone runs the command through VoiceOver or TalkBack over Bluetooth.

  5. 5

    Confirm

    A distinct vibration pattern tells your hand which command the ring heard.

The hand is the interface

Every command lives on skin you can feel without looking. Seven fixed commands, two personal shortcuts, and one emergency hold — separated by position and, for the emergency, by duration.

Index · tip · Fixed command

Confirm

Confirm — activate the focused item, answer a call, accept a suggestion. The "yes" of the whole system, on the finger wearing the ring.

  • —Brief tap: Confirm
  • Fixed command (7) — never moves
  • Personal shortcut (2) — yours to map
  • Emergency — five-second hold on the pinky tip

Meet the prototype

Everything below is labelled the way a lab notebook would label it: what is measured, what is simulated, what is a target, and what is still a plan.

Parts

  1. 1

    Ring shell. 3D-printed for the bench prototype; soft-touch polymer is the long-term aim.

  2. 2

    Three magnetometers. Low-cost sensors spaced around the band to localise the thumb magnet.

  3. 3

    Squeeze input. A deliberate squeeze of the band wakes the ring and opens the command window.

  4. 4

    Haptic motor. Plays a distinct confirmation pattern for each command.

  5. 5

    Bluetooth LE module. Talks to VoiceOver and TalkBack on the paired phone.

  6. 6

    Passive thumb magnet. Worn on the thumb; it has no battery and emits nothing.

Why nine commands?

Because the evidence says fewer, better-spaced targets beat many crowded ones.

91.3% of blind and low-vision screen-reader users rely on one on mobile, yet only 38% use braille output at all — and refreshable braille hardware runs from $799 to $15,500. Voice control is conditionally reliable: it fails in noise, broadcasts your business, and for atypical speech mainstream assistants have measured accuracy around 50–60%.

Tactiq's answer is deliberately small: nine commands on eight contact points, driven by the screen reader you already use. Text entry is excluded on purpose, and every command is recoverable — Undo has its own dedicated point instead of any delete gesture.

Why eight physical contact points, not more+−

The capacity analysis treats the hand as a channel: each extra contact point adds information but shrinks the landing zone a thumb has to hit. The analysis finds a knee at eight points — going to sixteen adds only about +0.31 bits of capacity while the worst command's accuracy collapses from 87% to roughly 50%.

For context: Apple's AssistiveTouch ships 4 gestures, Meta's sEMG wristband handles roughly 9, and EFRing reached 89.5% accuracy on 9. Nine commands is where reliable sits.

How magnetic localisation is expected to work+−

A passive magnet on the thumb creates a field that falls off with the cube of distance. Three magnetometers in the ring each read that field; solving the inverse problem gives the thumb's position. In simulation this resolves the thumb to about 1.65 mm at the array centre and about 4.4 mm off-centre — an order of magnitude finer than the 20–25 mm spacing between contact points.

The simulation assumes magnet tilt under ~12°, per-sensor gain calibration, and a minimum sensor standoff. Outside those conditions the error grows.

What the bench experiment will test+−

The honest risk in the design is not sensor noise — it is thumb aim. The bench experiment (August–October 2026) therefore measures real thumbs first: per-contact accuracy across repeated prompted trials, false activations per hour of ordinary wear, and how quickly the squeeze-wake window feels natural. The protocol and targets were written down before the experiment, so results cannot quietly become claims.

What remains uncertain+−
  • Whether per-contact accuracy holds across different hand sizes and nail lengths.
  • How often everyday movement squeezes the ring by accident.
  • Battery life under realistic duty cycles — not yet measured.
  • Comfort of all-day wear with the thumb magnet.

Sources

  • WebAIM Screen Reader Survey #10 (2024) — mobile screen-reader and braille usage

Questions people actually ask

How does the ring know which point I tapped?+−

A passive magnet and three low-cost magnetometers in the ring localize the thumb using the inverse-cube law. In simulation that resolves position to about 1.65 mm at the array centre — against 20–25 mm between contact points. It all happens on-device: no camera, no microphone, no cloud round-trip. These are simulation results; the bench experiment (August–October 2026) measures real thumbs.

Do I need to look at my phone to use it?+−

No — that’s the whole point. Nine fixed commands on the fingers you can always feel drive VoiceOver or TalkBack, and a distinct haptic pattern confirms each one. An optional single earbud (one ear only — ambient sound is how blind users read the street) adds spoken detail when you want it.

What stops it firing in my pocket or mid-conversation?+−

The ring is idle until you deliberately squeeze the ring body, which opens a short command window. The pre-registered design target is at most one false activation per hour. Emergency is stricter still: a sustained 5-second hold on the pinky tip — never a tap count — so it cannot fire by accident.

Why only nine commands? Can it type?+−

Deliberately not. Our capacity analysis found a knee at eight contact points — going to sixteen adds only ~0.31 bits of information but collapses worst-command accuracy from 87% to roughly 50%. Text entry and any delete or clear-field gesture are excluded by design: every Tactiq command is recoverable, and Undo has its own dedicated point.

Does it replace VoiceOver or TalkBack?+−

Never — it augments them over Bluetooth. Your screen reader stays exactly as you configured it; Tactiq just gives its most-used actions a physical home on one hand, so the other hand is free for a cane or a guide-dog harness.

When does it ship and how much does it cost?+−

It doesn’t — yet. Tactiq is a student research project: the bench experiment runs August–October 2026, the AUSSEF submission is due 11 November 2026, and ISEF 2027 is the pathway after that. The bench prototype costs under $60 in parts, and the positioning aim is consumer-electronics pricing — there is deliberately no firm retail price to promise.

Is Tactiq only for blind or low-vision users?+−

Blind and low-vision users are who we design for first — one-handed, silent, eyes-free control is the core requirement. The same properties help older and motor-impaired users, and anyone whose eyes and hands are busy.

Is my data private?+−

Yes. Tap detection runs on the ring itself, so your movements never leave your hand unless you choose to sync shortcut layouts. We collect the minimum needed to run your account, and never sell your data.

Something else? Email the project.

Designed around ordinary components

The bench prototype is built from off-the-shelf parts for under $60 — three magnetometers, a small magnet, a haptic motor and a Bluetooth module. That is the point of the design: nothing in it requires exotic hardware.

The long-term aim is consumer-electronics pricing — the kind of money people spend on earbuds, not the $799–$15,500 of refreshable braille hardware. No retail price or release date has been confirmed, and there is nothing to buy today.
